title: Pygmalion
tagline: Language is the sharpest tool of power — and the hardest to unlearn.

scenes.text: London, 1912. George Bernard Shaw — playwright, critic, socialist, controversialist — prepares to write a play about the most powerful weapon in English society: the English language itself. It is impossible, he believes, for an Englishman to open his mouth without making some other Englishman hate or despise him.

scenes.speaker: George Bernard Shaw
scenes.text: The class system is written into the vowels. Change the accent and you change the person — or do you? That is the question.

challenge.instruction: Pygmalion opens on a wet night in Covent Garden, a few streets from the slums of Seven Dials. Light every lamp on the streets where Eliza sells her flowers.
challenge.fact: My Fair Lady (1956) ran for 2,717 performances on Broadway. Shaw famously wrote his own stage directions to prevent producers from adding a romantic happy ending.

scenes.text: Pygmalion was based on the myth of the sculptor who fell in love with his creation — reimagined as Professor Higgins transforming Cockney flower seller Eliza Doolittle into a duchess through elocution lessons.

scenes.speaker: Henry Higgins
scenes.text: In six months I can pass this guttersnipe off as a duchess at an ambassador's garden party.

scenes.speaker: George Bernard Shaw
scenes.text: And the audience will laugh. And then go home and speak with the very accent that signals their breeding — and think nothing of it.

challenge.instruction: Higgins can place a speaker within six miles by a single sound. Guess the five-letter word for what he means to change in Eliza.
challenge.fact: Shaw wrote 'Back to Methuselah' (1921), a five-play cycle running from Adam and Eve to the year 31,920. He was the first person to win both a Nobel Prize (1925) and an Academy Award (1938, for the screenplay of Pygmalion).

scenes.text: Shaw fought constantly with directors who wanted a happy ending — Higgins and Eliza united in romance. Shaw refused. The ending he wrote is deliberately ambiguous. Eliza walks away. She is not the professor's creation: she is her own.

scenes.speaker: George Bernard Shaw
scenes.text: A life spent making mistakes is not only more honourable but more useful than a life spent doing nothing.

challenge.instruction: A Hungarian phonetics expert approaches Eliza Doolittle at the ambassador's party. What does he conclude?
challenge.fact: Shaw's irony: Eliza succeeds so perfectly that the expert concludes she must be foreign nobility — her English is too refined for a native. Class is performance, not origin.

Shaw explicitly wrote that Eliza marries Freddy Eynsford-Hill, not Higgins. He was furious when stage productions implied a romance. His epilogue spells out that Higgins is too self-absorbed for love. The musical My Fair Lady contradicts Shaw's own ending.
challenge.instruction: Shaw's epilogue has been printed in raised dots. Read how Eliza's story ends.

scenes.speaker: George Bernard Shaw
scenes.text: This time the whole board is judged at once. Deploy Coco Chanel, Sergei Eisenstein and me, turn us public, then declare the Roadshow: the highest public Culture on the board when the round ends takes the prize.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 6 · Global Competition. Deploy your Great People, Go Public on each, then start the Roadshow and End Turn to win the round with the highest public Culture on the board.
challenge.fact: A Global Competition counts every public Great Person on the whole board; followers and face-down cards add nothing. It lasts one round, and the strongest player draws a reward: event cards, followers or a new Great Person.
